name: Projectile Launcher
description: Launch a projectile and see how speed, angle, gravity and quadratic air drag shape the trajectory. Trails persist so launches can be compared.

challenges.text: Hit the target flag — land within 3 % of its distance.
Without drag, fire two complementary angles (e.g. 30° and 60°) at the same speed: they share a range.
Repeat the same launch on a different planet: how do hang time and range scale with g?
Switch drag on: is 45° still the best angle for range? Find the new optimum.

name: Nonlinear Pendulum
description: θ̈ = −(g/L)·sin θ − b·θ̇ integrated with RK4 — no small-angle approximation. Drag the bob to set the release angle; a ghost bob follows the small-angle solution.

challenges.text: Measure the period at θ₀ ≤ 15° and again at θ₀ ≥ 150°. How far off is 2π√(L/g) for the big swing?
Double the length (1 m → 2 m): by what factor does the period change? Why √2?
Run it as a lab: from L and your measured small-angle period, compute g and compare with the slider.
Add damping: as the amplitude decays, does the period drift? In which direction and why?

name: Driven Spring–Mass Oscillator
description: m·ẍ = −k·x − c·ẋ + F₀·cos(2πf_d·t). Natural frequency, damping ratio, resonance and phase lag with a live x(t) trace and the resonance curve.

challenges.text: Tune f_d to the natural frequency f₀ = √(k/m)/2π and hold it there: watch the amplitude grow.
Turn driving off and set c so that ζ = c/(2√(km)) = 1: the mass returns with no overshoot.
Drive far above resonance (f_d > 2f₀): the mass moves opposite to the force — phase lag → 180°.
Lower c and watch the resonance curve: how do peak height and width relate to Q = √(km)/c?

name: Collision Carts
description: Two carts on a frictionless track. Set masses, velocities and the coefficient of restitution e, then compare momentum and kinetic energy before and after the collision.

params.label: Bouncy walls at the track ends

challenges.text: Equal masses, e = 1, one cart at rest: the carts swap velocities.
Set e = 0: the carts stick together. How much KE is lost, and where does it go?
Make the target cart ≥ 8× heavier and at rest: the light cart rebounds at almost its incoming speed.
Verify: momentum is conserved for every e, kinetic energy only when e = 1.

name: Orbit Designer
description: A satellite around Earth integrated with velocity-Verlet (symplectic). Explore circular, elliptical and escape trajectories, Kepler's laws and orbital energy.

params.label: Start distance from Earth's centre (×1000 km)
Time warp (simulated s per real s)

challenges.text: Find the speed that makes the orbit circular (e < 0.02) at your chosen distance. Compare with √(GM/r).
Raise the speed until the satellite escapes. Compare the threshold with √(2GM/r) = √2 × circular speed.
Complete a lap on two orbits with different semi-major axes: check that T²/a³ stays constant.
On an eccentric orbit compare the two shaded sweeps: equal areas in equal times — where is the satellite fastest?

name: Wave Superposition
description: Two sinusoidal waves and their sum. Same-direction waves show beats; counter-propagating waves build standing waves with nodes λ/2 apart. Click the canvas to move the probe.

challenges.text: Same direction, |f₁ − f₂| ≤ 0.3 Hz: count the beats at the probe — the beat frequency is |f₁ − f₂|.
Opposite directions with equal A and f: find the nodes and compare their spacing with λ/2.
Same direction, equal A and f, φ = 180°: complete destructive interference.
Opposite directions, unequal amplitudes: a partially standing wave. Relate envelope max/min to the SWR.

name: Electric Field & Potential
description: Click to place point charges (drag to move them). Field lines follow E = kΣq·r̂/r², equipotentials are contours of V = kΣq/r. Hover anywhere to read |E| and V.

challenges.text: Build a dipole (equal and opposite charges). Why are the equipotentials perpendicular to the field lines everywhere?
Two like charges: hover to find the point where |E| ≈ 0. Where does it sit when the charges are unequal?
Place +2 nC and −1 nC: count the lines — how many leave the + charge without reaching the − charge, and where do they go?
Arrange + − + − on a square (a quadrupole). Hovering, compare how fast |E| falls with distance vs. a dipole.

name: Ideal Gas in a Box
description: Hard-disc molecules in a 2-D box (nm, ps, amu units). Pressure is measured from wall impulses, temperature from the mean kinetic energy, and the speed histogram is compared with the 2-D Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.

params.label: Box width (fraction of 100 nm) — moves a piston

challenges.text: Thermostat on: halve the box width — does the measured pressure double? (Boyle: PV = const at fixed T)
Fixed volume: double T — the pressure doubles too (Gay-Lussac). Check that PV/NkT stays ≈ 1.
Thermostat off: compress the box. Why does the gas heat up? (The moving piston does work on the molecules.)
Pack N = 400 molecules into the narrowest box: PV/NkT climbs above 1. Which ideal-gas assumption fails?

name: Special Relativity Lab
description: A light clock aboard a moving ship: time dilation and length contraction follow from the invariance of c. The Minkowski diagram shows the ship's tilted axes and lines of simultaneity.

challenges.text: Find the speed at which γ = 2, so the ship's clock ticks at half the ground rate.
Push β to 0.98+: a muon (lifetime 2.2 µs) could only travel 660 m classically — read how far it gets with time dilation.
Events A and B are simultaneous for the ground (same ct). Which happens first for the ship, and why?
Check that (ct)² − x² of the ship's current event equals (cτ)² — the same interval in every frame.

name: Particle in a Box
description: An electron in an infinite square well: ψₙ = √(2/L)·sin(nπx/L), Eₙ = n²h²/(8mL²). Superpose two states and watch |ψ|² slosh as the phases rotate at different rates.

params.label: Playback (fs of physics per real s)
Show Re ψ and Im ψ

challenges.text: Show n = 4 alone (weight 0 or m = 0): count the nodes inside the well — always n − 1.
Mix n = 1 and m = 2 with equal weight: ⟨x⟩ oscillates with period h/(E₂ − E₁). Check it against the readout.
Halve L: by what factor do all energies change? Why does confinement cost energy?
With one state, |ψ|² is frozen while Re ψ and Im ψ rotate — explain why it is called a stationary state.

name: Blackbody Radiation
description: Planck's law for one or two temperatures, with Wien's peak marker, the visible band and the Stefan–Boltzmann total power.

challenges.text: Set T₁ = 5800 K (the Sun's photosphere): where does the peak fall relative to the visible band? Coincidence?
Make T₂ exactly twice T₁ and compare the total powers: the ratio should be 2⁴ = 16.
Find the lowest temperature at which more than 0.1 % of the power is visible — the onset of 'red hot'.
The cosmic microwave background is a 2.7 K blackbody. Use Wien's law to predict its peak wavelength (in mm).

name: Atom Builder
description: Assemble a nucleus and its electron cloud: protons choose the element, neutrons the isotope, electrons the charge. Bohr shells follow the Aufbau electron configuration, and a Segrè chart shows where the nucleus sits relative to the band of stability.

challenges.text: Build a neutral, stable carbon-13 atom (Z = 6, N = 7, 6 electrons).
Make the sodium cation Na⁺ — which noble gas does its configuration match?
Find a noble gas: a neutral atom whose outer shell is completely filled.
For an element with Z ≥ 50, find a neutron number inside the band of stability. Why do heavy nuclei need N > Z?

name: Periodic Trends Explorer
description: A periodic table (H → Rn) colour-coded by atomic radius, first ionisation energy, electronegativity or electron affinity. Hover for values, click to select an element and read how the property changes across its period and down its group.

params.label: Tint the selected period and group

challenges.text: Show electronegativity and click the most electronegative element.
Show atomic radius and click the largest atom of period 3.
Show ionisation energy and click N, then O: why does IE drop even though Z increases?
Show electron affinity and click the element that releases the most energy when it gains an electron (it is not fluorine!).

name: Reaction Kinetics Lab
description: A → P with rate = k[A]ⁿ (n = 0, 1, 2) and k = A·e^(−Ea/RT). Watch [A](t) with the three linearised plots and the half-life, probe the Arrhenius temperature dependence, and identify the order of a hidden 'mystery sample'.

params.label: log₁₀ of the pre-exponential factor A

challenges.text: Changing only T, find the temperature that doubles k relative to the reference (k/k_ref = 2). Is it 10 K hotter?
Press 'Mystery sample', pick the order whose linearised plot is straight (R² → 1), then 'Check order'.
In second order, double [A]₀ and watch the half-life halve (in first order it would not change).
At the reference temperature, lower Ea by ≥ 20 kJ/mol (a catalyst). Compare the speed-up with e^(ΔEa/RT).

name: Chemical Equilibrium & Le Chatelier
description: A reversible reaction integrated from mass-action kinetics: concentrations relax until Q = K = kf/kr. Perturb the equilibrium — remove product, add reactant, compress, heat — and watch it shift the way Le Chatelier predicts.

params.label: Your prediction for K (type it before reading K)

challenges.text: Wait for equilibrium, then remove product: the reaction makes more of it until Q = K again.
Change kf or kr, predict K = kf/kr and type it into the box — within 2 %.
At equilibrium, compress the mixture: it shifts toward the side with fewer moles (more product here).
With an exothermic reaction (ΔH < 0) at equilibrium, heat it: K drops and product decomposes.

name: Titration Curves
description: pH versus titrant volume for strong/weak acids and bases, solved exactly from the charge balance. See the buffer region, the half-equivalence point (pH = pKa), the equivalence jump, and whether your indicator changes colour in the right place.

params.label: pKa of the weak acid (or of the weak base's conjugate acid)

challenges.text: Stop the titrant within 0.3 mL of the equivalence volume (moles of titrant = moles of analyte).
Weak acid or base: park at half-equivalence and read pH = pKa straight off the curve.
For a weak acid or weak base titration choose an indicator whose colour change lies inside the steep jump (±2 % of the equivalence volume).
Hit equivalence in both a weak-acid and a weak-base titration: why is one above pH 7 and the other below?

name: Radioactive Decay
description: Every nucleus decays at random with probability λ·Δt per step — the jagged count is compared with the smooth N₀e^(−λt). Switch on a decay chain (parent → daughter → stable) and watch the daughter rise, peak and fade (Bateman equations).

params.label: Time warp (simulated s per real s)

challenges.text: Type your prediction for the % remaining after 3 half-lives, then let the sample get there.
Turn the chain on and watch the daughter population rise, peak and fall away again.
Run a tiny sample (N₀ ≤ 100) and a big one (N₀ ≥ 1000) past 2 half-lives: which hugs the smooth curve? (noise ∝ √N)
Chain with a short-lived daughter (t½,D ≤ t½,P/8): after a few daughter half-lives its activity locks onto the parent's — transient equilibrium.

name: Function Plotter
description: Type any f(x) with parameters a, b, c. Pan and zoom, mark zeros and extrema, and overlay the numerical derivative f′(x).

challenges.text: With a = b = 1, slide c until the two outer zeros merge into a single touching point (a double root). What is f′ there?
Overlay f′(x): check that every maximum of f sits where f′ crosses zero from + to −, and every minimum where it crosses from − to +.
Type a formula using ln, sqrt or 1/(x−a). Explain every gap and asymptote in the picture from the domain of f.
Zoom in (mouse wheel) on any smooth point until the curve looks like a straight line — local linearity is why derivatives work.

name: Derivative Explorer
description: Watch the secant through x₀ and x₀ + h become the tangent as h → 0, and compare the difference quotient with f′(x₀).

challenges.text: For x³ − 3x at x₀ = 1 (where f′ = 0), slide h toward 0 until the forward quotient is within 0.01 of f′. Roughly which h did it take?
Switch to the central quotient and repeat: the error now falls like h² instead of h. Read the slope off the log–log inset.
Choose |x| with x₀ = 0: forward gives +1, backward −1, central 0. Explain why no tangent line exists there.
For eˣ, verify at several x₀ that the tangent slope equals the height f(x₀).

name: Riemann Sums & Numerical Integration
description: Approximate ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx with left, right, midpoint, trapezoid or Simpson rules and watch how fast each error shrinks as n grows.

challenges.text: Double n and watch the error: it roughly halves for left/right, quarters for midpoint/trapezoid and drops ~16× for Simpson. Confirm with the Error(n)/Error(2n) readout.
On x² the midpoint error is about half the trapezoid error and has the opposite sign. Explain both facts with concavity.
Simpson's rule is exact for cubics: choose x³ − x with n = 2 and check the error is (numerically) zero.
Choose 1/x with a = −1, b = 1. Why can no n rescue the estimate — what kind of integral is this?

name: Taylor Series Explorer
description: Build Taylor polynomials of growing degree about a centre a, and see where they converge to f — and where no degree will ever help.

challenges.text: Pick ln(1 + x) at a = 0 and push n to 30. Why does Tₙ track f only on (−1, 1] no matter how large n gets?
For 1/(1 − x), move the centre a: the convergence interval always ends at x = 1. Explain it with the distance to the singularity.
arctan has no real singularity, yet its series at a = 0 fails beyond |x| = 1. What limits it? (Think complex plane: ±i.)
sin at a = 0 uses only odd powers, cos only even. Check the coefficient readout and relate it to the symmetry of each function.

name: 2×2 Matrix Transformations
description: See a 2×2 matrix act on the plane: transformed grid, unit square, basis vectors, eigenvectors with eigenvalues and the determinant as signed area.

challenges.text: Make det A = 0 (e.g. the projection preset). What happens to the grid, and why can the map not be undone?
A shear has a single eigenvector direction. Find it on screen and explain why λ = 1 appears twice but gives only one direction.
Rotation by 45° shows no real eigenvectors. Animate I → A: is there any direction that is never turned?
For the symmetric matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] the eigenvectors are perpendicular. Nudge one slider to make A non-symmetric — does that survive?

name: Probability Distribution Explorer
description: Shape classic distributions, draw random samples, and watch the Central Limit Theorem turn means of skewed data into a bell curve.

params.label: CLT mode: histogram of sample means

challenges.text: Pick the (very skewed) exponential, switch on CLT mode and raise k. From what k on do the sample means look bell-shaped?
Binomial with large n: for which p does the pmf look normal, and when does it look like a Poisson instead?
Compare Student t with ν = 1 against the normal and sample repeatedly: why does the sample variance never settle down?
In CLT mode compare the predicted σ/√k with the observed spread of the means for k = 1, 4, 16 and 64.

name: Least-Squares Regression Lab
description: Click to place points, drag to move them. Fit polynomials by least squares and watch residuals, R², RMSE — and catch overfitting with leave-one-out error.

challenges.text: With ~8 noisy points raise the degree to 5: training RMSE falls but leave-one-out RMSE rises — overfitting. Which degree minimises the LOO error?
Add one far-away point and drag it around. How much does a degree-1 line pivot? Which points have the most leverage, and why?
Generate the parabola pattern and fit degree 1: R² is near 0 despite an obvious pattern. What does R² actually measure?
Check in the readout that the residuals of any least-squares fit with an intercept sum to zero. Why must that happen?

name: Fourier Series & Epicycles
description: Add harmonics one at a time: rotating epicycles trace the partial sum of a square, sawtooth, triangle or pulse wave. Watch Gibbs ringing and Parseval's energy count.

challenges.text: Raise N for the square wave: the ringing gets narrower but the overshoot stays ≈ 9 % of the jump. That is the Gibbs phenomenon — why doesn't it vanish?
Compare the coefficient bars: square and sawtooth amplitudes decay like 1/n, the triangle like 1/n². Which feature of f sets the rate?
How many harmonics does the triangle need to capture 99 % of the energy? And the square wave? (Parseval readout.)
Why does the square wave contain only odd harmonics? Switch to the pulse and watch even harmonics appear.

name: Phase Portrait Lab
description: Vector field, nullclines and RK4 trajectories for classic 2-D autonomous systems. Click anywhere to launch a trajectory from that initial condition.

params.label: p₁ = α prey growth · c damping · μ

challenges.text: Predator–prey: every click gives a closed loop around (γ, α). The linearisation only says 'centre' — use the conserved H = x − γ·ln x + y − α·ln y to argue the loops really close.
Damped pendulum: click near θ = π (inverted). Which starts fall to θ = 0 and which to θ = 2π? Sketch the separatrix between the basins.
van der Pol: start inside and outside the loop — both trajectories end on the same limit cycle. Change μ and describe how its shape changes.
Linear system: use the matrix sliders to produce a saddle, a centre and a stable spiral; relate each to the trace/determinant readout.

name: Graph Algorithms Visualiser
description: Step through BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Prim's MST and topological sort on random or preset graphs. Click nodes to choose the source and the target.

challenges.text: Find a source/target pair where BFS (fewest edges) and Dijkstra (least total weight) choose different routes. Why can both be called 'shortest'?
Run Prim from two different sources: the total MST weight is identical. Is the tree itself always identical? When could it differ?
Before stepping, predict the DFS visit order from the drawing (lowest-numbered neighbour first). Were you right?
On the DAG, is the topological order unique? Find two nodes that could be swapped and explain where Kahn's algorithm had a free choice.

name: Modular Arithmetic Clock
description: Residues mod n on a circle: step through multiples or powers of a to reveal cycles, gcd structure, units, inverses and primes.

challenges.text: Set n = 12. For which a do the multiples of a visit every point? Relate the number of points hit to gcd(a, 12).
Choose a prime n: every non-zero residue is a unit and the multiplication table has no zeros inside. Why does primality force this?
With n = 13, record the multiplicative order of several units a. Check that each one divides φ(13) = 12 (Lagrange's theorem).
Find a primitive root mod 13: an a whose powers visit all 12 units. How many primitive roots does 13 have?

name: Gradient Descent Explorer
description: Roll SGD, momentum or Adam down 2-D loss surfaces drawn as log-spaced contour heatmaps. Click anywhere on the surface to choose where the optimiser starts.

challenges.text: Make the optimiser diverge: raise η until the loss explodes. On the bowl, at what η does SGD blow up — and why exactly that value?
On the ravine, reach loss < 0.01 with plain SGD and then with momentum (same η). Which one zig-zags, and which needs fewer steps?
Use “Start on saddle ridge”: SGD slides into the saddle point and stalls. Add gradient noise σ > 0 — what frees it, and why is this good news for SGD?
Reach loss < 0.001 inside the curved Rosenbrock valley within 3000 steps. Compare SGD and Adam.

name: Perceptron Learning Rule
description: Rosenblatt's perceptron learns a linear decision boundary one mistake at a time. See why it must converge on separable data — and why XOR defeats it.

challenges.text: Train on the separable data until a full epoch has zero mistakes. How many epochs did it take, and what guarantees that it stops?
Switch to XOR and train for 200+ epochs. Why can no single line ever separate the classes?
Reset weights and retrain with η = 0.01, then η = 1.0 on the same data. Does η change the epoch count or the final boundary? Explain (hint: w starts at 0).
Click points to flip their labels until training never converges. What is the smallest number of flips that breaks separability here?

name: Neural Network Playground
description: A tiny multilayer perceptron trained live with hand-written forward and backward passes. Shape the data, the architecture and η — and watch the decision boundary form.

challenges.text: Solve XOR (test accuracy ≥ 95 %) with ONE hidden layer. What is the fewest units that still works, and why does a single unit fail?
Fit the two spirals to ≥ 90 % test accuracy. Which depth / width / activation gets there fastest?
With ReLU, push η up until training stalls or the weights overflow. Then find the largest η that still trains. What happened to the hidden units?
Set noise to 0.5 and train for a long time: train and test accuracy separate. Which single change shrinks the gap most?

name: k-Means Clustering
description: Lloyd's algorithm one half-step at a time: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move every centroid to the mean of its members. Explore initialisation, local minima and the elbow heuristic.

challenges.text: Step assign → update until the centroids stop moving. Why can the inertia never go up between half-steps?
Compute the elbow plot on the blobs, pick the k at the bend, set it and converge. Does it match the hidden number of blobs?
With random init on the blobs, re-initialise until two centroids end up sharing one blob (a local minimum). Does k-means++ avoid it?
Cluster the two moons with k = 2. Why does k-means cut them the 'wrong' way — which assumption about cluster shape is violated?

name: Self-Attention Visualiser
description: Scaled dot-product self-attention over a toy sentence: hash-based token embeddings + sinusoidal positions, seeded Wq/Wk per head. Click a token to see where it looks.

params.label: Sentence
params.value: the robot picked up the red ball because it was closest

challenges.text: Turn on the causal mask: which half of the matrix vanishes, and why must a decoder (GPT-style) train with it?
Sweep T from 0.1 to 5. Describe the rows at both extremes (one-hot vs. uniform). What role does the √d in the real formula play?
Compare Head 1 and Head 2 for the same query token. Do they pick different positions? Why do transformers use several heads?
Type a sentence with a repeated word. Does a word attend strongly to its own copy? Explain using how the embeddings are built.

name: n-gram Language Model
description: Count-based next-word prediction trained on a tiny corpus about science and robots. Change n, type a prefix, sample continuations and watch sparsity bite.

params.label: n (predicts from the previous n − 1 words)

challenges.text: Set n = 4, smoothing = None, and type a 3-word prefix the corpus never contains. What does the model predict, and why is that fatal for perplexity?
With interpolated smoothing, visit n = 1, 2, 3, 4 and compare held-out perplexity. Why doesn't a bigger n always win on a tiny corpus?
Generate at temperature 0.1 and again at 2.0. Compare fluency vs. variety — what does T do to the distribution?
At n = 4 generate from “robots can”. Does the model just copy the corpus? Explain the link between n, data size and memorisation.

name: Multi-Armed Bandit
description: k slot machines with hidden payout rates. Balance exploring and exploiting with ε-greedy, UCB1 or Thompson sampling — or pull the arms yourself and compete.

challenges.text: Pull the arms by hand (click them) 30 times before any auto-play. Which arm do you think is best, and how sure are you?
Set ε = 0 (pure greedy) and auto-play 500 pulls. Reveal the means: did it lock onto a sub-optimal arm? Why can it never recover?
Reach ≥ 80 % optimal-arm pulls after 1000+ pulls with any strategy.
On the same bandit run UCB1 and Thompson to 2000 pulls each (Reset stats in between). Whose regret curve flattens first, and why is regret sub-linear at all?

name: Gridworld: Q-learning vs SARSA
description: Temporal-difference control on a gridworld with a cliff. Watch Q-values and the greedy policy emerge, and see why off-policy Q-learning walks the edge while on-policy SARSA plays it safe.

challenges.text: Reach the goal in at least one episode.
On the cliff, train Q-learning and then SARSA (ε = 0.1) for 300 episodes each. Which greedy path hugs the cliff, which stays high — and why does on-policy learning care about ε?
Reset Q with ε = 0 from the start. Does the agent ever find the goal? Now set ε = 0 only after training — what changes?
Set γ = 0.3 on the maze and train. Why do cells far from the goal stay 'blind' — what does γ do to the planning horizon?

name: LLM Agent Loop Simulator
description: Step through a ReAct-style agent: Thought → Action (tool call) → Observation. Choose the tools yourself and discover how wrong calls, missing memory and no step budget turn into loops and failures.

options.label: I do (click a tool each step)

challenges.text: Complete any goal with zero wrong tool calls. Which clue in each Thought told you the right tool?
Call the same wrong tool three times in a row. What should a production agent do when it notices repeated identical actions?
Set the step budget to 4 and try the research goal. Why do agents need a termination rule, and what should they return when the budget runs out?
Turn scratchpad memory off on the trip goal and run it. Where does the agent break down, and how do real agents fix this (context window vs. external memory)?

name: Tokenizer Lab (BPE)
description: Train byte-pair encoding on a small corpus and watch merges turn characters into sub-words. Compare with whitespace, word and character tokenisation.

params.label: Text to tokenise
params.value: the robots unlocked the laboratory doors unexpectedly

challenges.text: Type a word with a character the corpus never saw (e.g. “café” or digits). What does each tokeniser do with it, and why is that a problem for a model?
Slide merges from 0 to 200 and watch tokens-per-character. Where do the gains flatten, and why?
Find an English word that is still split into 4+ BPE tokens at 190+ merges. Why do rare words fragment while common ones become single tokens?
Compare word-level and BPE vocabulary sizes on this corpus. Which handles a brand-new word better, and at what cost?

name: PID Controller Lab
description: Tune P, I and D gains on three honest plants — a hovering drone (gravity is a constant load), a first-order DC motor and a slow heater with dead time — and read off overshoot, rise time, settling time and steady-state error.

options.label: DC motor speed (×10 rad/s) — first order
Heater ΔT (×10 °C) — slow, with dead time

challenges.text: Drone with Ki = 0: it hovers below the setpoint because gravity is a constant load. Add just enough Ki to remove the steady-state error. Why can P alone never fix it?
Tune the drone so a setpoint step of ≥ 2 m (use the Step setpoint button) has ≤ 5 % overshoot and a 10–90 % rise time under 1.5 s.
With Ki > 0 and anti-windup off, make a saturated climb overshoot by more than 30 %. Then switch anti-windup on, step again, and cut that overshoot by at least 30 %.
Switch to the heater and raise Kp until the dead time makes it oscillate without decaying — that is the ultimate gain that Ziegler–Nichols tuning starts from.

name: Planar Robot Arm — Inverse Kinematics
description: Drag the target: a 2-link arm solves inverse kinematics analytically (two elbow solutions, a donut-shaped workspace, singular at full stretch). Add a third link and watch an iterative Jacobian-transpose solver converge instead.

challenges.text: Park the target somewhere reachable and flip Elbow up/down a few times: same hand position, different joint angles. Why does 2-link IK have exactly two answers — and where does it have only one?
Drag the target to the outer rim of the workspace and watch manipulability fall towards 0. What happens to the joint speeds needed for a small hand motion there?
Make L1 at least 0.3 m longer than L2 and try to touch the base: the inner hole of the annulus is unreachable. What sets its radius?
Enable the 3rd link and drag the target around: now infinitely many joint solutions exist. What decides which one the iterative solver lands on?

name: Differential-Drive Robot
description: Drive a two-wheeled robot with independent wheel speeds (sliders, or arrow keys after clicking the canvas). See the instantaneous centre of curvature and turning radius, dead-reckoning drift, and a pure-pursuit autopilot chasing waypoints.

challenges.text: Make the robot spin on the spot for a full second. Which wheel speeds give turning radius R = 0?
Set vL = 0.3, vR = 0.6, L = 0.4 and compute the turning radius R = (L/2)·(vR + vL)/(vR − vL) before checking the readout.
Reach all four waypoints by hand (sliders or arrow keys) with the autopilot off.
Let the autopilot finish the course twice (Reset pose in between): once with a tiny lookahead, once with a huge one. Which setting cuts corners and which one weaves?

name: Path Planning Playground
description: Paint obstacles, then watch BFS, Dijkstra, A* and greedy best-first expand their frontiers cell by cell — or grow a rapidly-exploring random tree. Compare nodes expanded against path cost and the true optimum.

challenges.text: Build (or keep) a U-shaped pocket that opens towards the start and run Greedy best-first: it dives in and comes out with a path ≥ 15 % longer than optimal. Then run A* on the same map.
Run Dijkstra and then A* (Manhattan or Euclidean) on the same map: A* expands under 70 % of the nodes yet finds the same optimal cost. Why does an admissible heuristic guarantee this?
Turn on diagonal moves and run BFS: its path costs more than Dijkstra's. Why does BFS stop being optimal as soon as step costs differ?
Run RRT three times on the same map (press ▶ Run again after it finishes). The path changes every time — what does RRT guarantee, and what doesn't it?

name: Kalman Filter Tracker
description: A constant-velocity Kalman filter tracks a maneuvering target through noisy, sometimes missing measurements. Tune the process noise q and sensor noise R and watch the ±2σ belief band breathe.

params.label: Sensor noise σ (m) — true and assumed

challenges.text: Tune q so the filter's RMSE drops below half of the raw sensor's RMSE while the target is maneuvering.
Set log q ≤ −2 and watch the estimate lag behind every turn; set log q ≥ 1 and it just copies the noise. Then find the sweet spot in between (RMSE < 60 % of the sensor's).
Push dropout to 0.7 or more: the ±2σ band grows during prediction-only steps and snaps shut on each measurement. Why does uncertainty keep growing without data?
Make σ huge: the Kalman gain → 0 and the filter trusts only its motion model. Make σ tiny: K → 1 and it copies the sensor. Explain both regimes in your own words.

name: Robot Behaviour State Machine
description: A vacuum robot driven by a finite-state machine. Edit the transition table, inject sensor events, and watch what happens when an event arrives that no transition handles — the robustness lesson every robot learns the hard way.

params.label: AvoidObstacle returns to the previous state (history)
Battery drain while moving (% per s)

challenges.text: Inject a fault while Charging: nothing happens, because that table cell is empty. Make every state except Error handle fault → Error.
Let the battery run low (or inject low_battery), then watch the robot hit an obstacle on its way home: bump has no transition from ReturnToDock, so it grinds in place. Add one.

After your fix the robot dodges the obstacle but then forgets it was heading home. Turn on the history option so AvoidObstacle returns to the previous state — the problem hierarchical state machines solve.
Review every empty cell: for each, decide whether ignoring the event is safe (e.g. charged while Exploring) or a latent bug. Which cells would you fill, and with what?

name: Truth Table & Equivalence Lab
description: Type any propositional formula (¬ ∧ ∨ → ↔ ⊕, or ASCII ~ & | -> <-> ^, or the words not/and/or). Get the full truth table with sub-formula columns, a shaded Venn diagram and a Karnaugh map, and test equivalence against a second formula.

challenges.text: Write a tautology that uses three different variables and at least one → (hypothetical syllogism is one; find another).
Verify De Morgan's law ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q, then check its dual by swapping ∧ and ∨ in both formulas.
Show that p ⊕ q is exactly the negation of p ↔ q (the readout will say 'negations of each other').
Build a contradiction using only → and ¬ (no ∧, ∨, ⊕ or ↔).

name: Trolley Problem Laboratory
description: Eight variations on the trolley problem — switch, footbridge, loop, surgeon, self-sacrifice, uncertainty, numbers and loyalty. Choose, watch the consequences play out, and see which moral principles your pattern of answers fits best. There are no right answers here, only reasons.

challenges.text: Work through all eight dilemmas and read your inferred profile and the tensions it flags.
If you pulled the lever in the Switch but not in the Loop (or vice versa): write down the one feature that changed your mind, and ask whether it would survive a surgeon-style case.
Find your own threshold in dilemma 7: re-answer it with at least two different numbers until you locate the smallest crowd for which diverting feels right.
Restart and answer every dilemma as a strict act-utilitarian would. Which theory does the fit report, and which 'tensions' disappear?

name: Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma
description: Play the iterated prisoner's dilemma against classic strategies, run an Axelrod-style round-robin tournament with noisy moves, and watch replicator dynamics decide which strategies survive in a population.

params.label: S — sucker's payoff (cooperate, get defected on)

challenges.text: Over 20+ rounds against Tit-for-Tat, finish with a higher score than it. Then ask: did 'winning' earn you more than steady mutual cooperation would have?
Set noise to 8 % or more and run the tournament. Why does Grim Trigger collapse while Generous Tit-for-Tat holds up?
Raise S above P (being exploited now beats mutual defection — a snowdrift / chicken game) and run the tournament. Does Always-Defect still win? Why is it no longer a dilemma?
Run evolution from equal shares with 0 noise, then with ≥ 5 % noise for 30+ time units. Who takes over, and why does noise change the winner?

name: Veil of Ignorance
description: Design the income distribution of a five-citizen society without knowing which citizen you will be. Compare Rawls's maximin, the utilitarian average, the Gini coefficient and log-utility — then drop the veil and find out where you landed.

params.label: Total income of the five (k$ / year)
Risk aversion η (CRRA; η = 1 is log utility)
Birth lottery favours poorer positions (2 : 1 odds)

challenges.text: Find a distribution where the utilitarian average is high but the poorest citizen gets under 5 %. Which principle would you choose behind the veil — and does your answer change with η?
Dial in a distribution with Gini ≈ 0.50 (± 0.02) and compare it with the US-like preset.
Drop the veil ten times. How does your average outcome compare with the mean income — and with the middle citizen?
Okun's leaky bucket: suppose every 10 % of income you redistribute destroys 2 % of the total. Would a maximin chooser still equalise completely? Where would they stop, and why?

name: Bayesian Belief Updating
description: A medical test on 1 000 people drawn as natural frequencies: see how a rare condition turns a 'very accurate' test into mostly false positives, then add tests one at a time to watch belief update sequentially.

challenges.text: Set prior 1 %, sensitivity 99 %, specificity 95 % and guess P(condition | positive) before reading it. Most doctors guess above 90 %.
How many independent positive tests does it take for belief to pass 99 %? Add them one at a time and watch the curve.
With a 1 % prior, which helps the posterior more: sensitivity 90 → 99 % or specificity 90 → 99 %? Test both and explain it with the grid.
After two positives, add a negative test. Does belief fall all the way back to the prior? Why not?

name: Sorites Paradox & Vagueness Lab
description: Remove grains from a heap one at a time. Compare four philosophical theories of vagueness (Epistemicism, Supervaluationism, Fuzzy/Degree theory, Contextualism) and see how each resolves the Sorites chain.

challenges.text: Switch to Supervaluationism and place n inside the borderline zone [L, U]. Observe that v(Heap(n)) is indeterminate while v(Heap(n) ∨ ¬Heap(n)) is still 1 (super-true).
In Fuzzy mode with Łukasiewicz logic, widen [L, U] so each step premise H(k)→H(k−1) has truth ≥ 0.97, yet the chained argument truth from 100 down to 0 drops to 0.
Use the '−1 grain (forced march)' button at least 10 times to march across the boundary and observe contextual shift / truth erosion.
In Epistemicism mode, find the exact grain k* where H(k*) = 1 and H(k*−1) = 0.

name: Argument Mapper & Defeat Calculus
description: Map linked vs. convergent premises, rebutting defeaters, and Pollock-style undercutting defeaters. Adjust credence in each node or click nodes on the canvas to watch support propagate to the conclusion.

challenges.text: In Pollock's Red Light, activate the red-light undercutter (U1 ≥ 0.8, R1 ≤ 0.15) so conclusion credence drops below 0.25 even though 'looks red' (P1) stays ≥ 0.85.
In Pollock's Red Light, raise the counter-defeater R1 ≥ 0.85 while U1 ≥ 0.8 to reinstate the perceptual warrant and bring conclusion credence above 0.70.
Drop P2 to 0.10 while P1 is 0.90, and compare 'Force linked' vs. 'Force convergent' modes to see why linked arguments fail on their weakest premise while convergent arguments survive.

name: Mandarin Tone & Pitch Contour Studio
description: Visualize and sculpt Mandarin Chinese pitch contours on Y. R. Chao's 5-level scale (1–5), inspect Tone Sandhi transformations (3+3→2+3, 一 yī, 不 bù), and test your contour accuracy.

options.label: Sandhi 不 bù — 不对 bù duì → bú duì
Sandhi 一 yī — 一定 yī dìng → yí dìng

challenges.text: Select 马 mǎ (Tone 3, 214) and sculpt the dipping pitch curve to achieve ≥ 90% contour match.
Switch to 你好 (nǐ hǎo → ní hǎo) and match the 3+3 → 2+3 sandhi contour (≥ 88% match).
Explore both 不对 (bú duì) and 一定 (yí dìng) sandhi patterns and press '🔊 Hear Mandarin'.

name: Arabic Abjad & Hanzi Radical Tracing Studio
description: Master right-to-left Arabic Abjad contextual letterforms (Isolated, Initial, Medial, Final + Harakat) and Chinese Hanzi radical decomposition & stroke order rules by tracing on the interactive calligrapher's slate.

options.label: ج Jīm (/dʒ/) — Brow + bowl + inner dot

challenges.text: Trace along the guide strokes on the calligraphy slate with your mouse or finger (≥ 70% path coverage).
In Arabic mode, inspect ع (ʿAyn) and ه (Hāʾ) across all 4 contextual positions and hear their pronunciation.
Switch to Mandarin Hanzi mode, select 清 (qīng), and step through all strokes to see 氵 + 青 decomposition.

name: European Grammar & Conjugation Matrix (German · Italian · French)
description: Compare German 4-case declensions & V2/Nebensatz word order with Italian and French tense/mood conjugation grids (Presente, Passato Prossimo/Passé Composé, Imperfetto, Subjunctive, plus French Liaison ‿).

options.label: Presente / Présent  |  DE: Hauptsatz (V2 Main Clause)
Passato Prossimo / Passé Composé  |  DE: Nebensatz (Verb-Final)

challenges.text: In German mode, toggle between Hauptsatz (V2) and Nebensatz (Verb-Final) and hear the spoken sentence.
Switch to Italian, inspect the Congiuntivo (subjunctive) across all 6 persons, and run a Morphological Drill.
Switch to French, explore aller in Passé Composé (être auxiliary + participle agreement + liaison ‿).

name: Arabic Triliteral Root (Jizr) & Pattern (Wazn) Weaver
description: Weave 3-consonant Arabic roots (Jizr جذر) into Verb Forms I–X and nominal templates (Wazn وزن) on an interactive morphological loom to see how non-concatenative morphology generates entire word families.

options.label: Form V: تَفَعَّلَ (tafaʿʿala) — Reflexive of II
Place Noun: مَفْعَل (mafʿal) — Place of Action

challenges.text: Select root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m) and compare Form I عَلِمَ (he knew), Form II عَلَّمَ (he taught), and Form V تَعَلَّمَ (he learned).
Weave the Place Noun pattern مَفْعَل (mafʿal) across ك-ت-ب (maktab office) and د-ر-س (madrasa school).
Weave Form X اِسْتَفْعَلَ (istafʿala) and press '🔊 Hear Arabic Word' to hear the requestative prefix ista-.

name: Polyglot Immersion Roleplay Deck (5 Languages)
description: Practice real-world situational conversations across Mandarin, German, Italian, French, and Arabic at 3 sociolinguistic registers (Casual, Polite Standard, Formal/Diplomatic) with native script, phonetic transcription, word-by-word gloss, and TTS playback.

challenges.text: Compare all 3 sociolinguistic registers (Casual, Polite Standard, Formal/Diplomatic) within any scene.
Complete a dialogue turn in at least 3 different languages (e.g., Mandarin, French, and Arabic) and hear their audio.
Switch to '3 · University Seminar & Debate' in Formal register and inspect the grammatical discourse markers.

name: Fourier Epicycles & Complex Phasors
description: Decompose periodic contours into rotating complex exponential phasors and inspect Gibbs ringing near discontinuities.

challenges.text: Increase Epicycle Count N ≥ 10 to sharpen the square-wave corner and observe Gibbs overshoot.
Drag the spectral probe on the canvas to measure local harmonic amplitude.
Vary Spectral Roll-Off α to transition between sawtooth (1/n) and triangle (1/n²) decay.

name: Lorenz Strange Attractor & Chaos
description: Integrate the 3D Lorenz atmospheric convection equations via RK4 and observe butterfly-wing chaos and positive Lyapunov exponents.

challenges.text: Tune Rayleigh Number ρ across the Hopf bifurcation at ρ ≈ 24.74.
Click the phase plane to launch a nearby trajectory and watch exponential divergence.
Stabilize the attractor into a damped fixed point by lowering ρ below 14.

name: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) Manifold
description: Explore rank-k matrix approximation, Eckart-Young Frobenius error bounds, and singular value spectrum decay.

challenges.text: Adjust Condition Number κ(A) to observe elliptical stretching of the quadratic form.
Click the manifold to project a test vector onto the top singular subspace.
Balance rank truncation k/r against spectral perturbation ε to minimize reconstruction loss.

name: 2D Reaction-Diffusion & Laplacian PDE Solver
description: Solve coupled parabolic PDEs on a 2D finite-difference stencil and inspect eigenmode smoothing and Turing patterns.

challenges.text: Tune Diffusivity D and Feed Rate F to transition from spots to labyrinthine stripes.
Click or drag on the 2D domain to impose a localized Dirichlet boundary impulse.
Drive the Laplacian toward homogeneous equilibrium by raising diffusivity D.

description: Simulate random walks on a directed stochastic graph and relate mixing time to the spectral gap 1 − |λ₂|.

challenges.text: Increase Out-Degree k to enlarge the algebraic connectivity λ₂ and accelerate mixing.
Click a vertex to inject probability mass and watch convergence to stationary distribution π.
Tune Ergodic Damping α to break periodicity and eliminate recurrent traps.

challenges.text: Vary Damping Factor α to compare quadratic convergence (α=1) vs over-relaxed oscillation.
Click near a saddle ridge on the canvas to observe basin boundary sensitivity.
Tune Levenberg Shift λ to stabilize iterations near singular Jacobian points.

Drag the complex plane probe to inspect local conformal magnification |f'(z)|.
Sweep Laurent Terms M to compare pure Joukowsky vs Kármán-Trefftz profiles.

Drag the probe on the canvas to inspect partial Dirichlet phasor cancellation.
Shift Re(s) away from 0.5 and observe why zero crossings break symmetry.

name: Cyclotomic Fields & Galois Group Permutations
description: Visualize primitive nth roots of unity on the unit circle and act on them via Frobenius automorphisms ζ ↦ ζᵏ.

challenges.text: Select coprime Automorphism Power k and Cyclotomic Degree n to generate the full multiplicative orbit.
Click the unit circle to select a root of unity and trace its Galois conjugate orbit.
Project onto the maximal real subfield ℚ(ζₙ + ζₙ⁻¹) using the projection slider.

description: Integrate geodesic spray on a curved 2-manifold and measure Jacobi field deviation and Gauss-Bonnet holonomy.

challenges.text: Compare geodesic convergence (K > 0) vs hyperbolic divergence (K < 0).
Click the manifold sphere to parallel-transport a tangent vector around a closed loop.
Locate conjugate antipodal focal points under positive Gaussian curvature.

name: Monte Carlo Importance Sampling & Variance Reduction
description: Compare naive uniform Monte Carlo against proposal-tilted importance sampling and inspect effective sample size (ESS).

challenges.text: Align Proposal Tilt μ_q with the target mode to maximize Effective Sample Size (ESS).
Drag the operating point along the likelihood ratio curve w(x) = p(x)/q(x).
Observe variance explosion when Proposal Scale σ_q is narrower than target tails.

name: Linear Programming Polytope & Simplex Pivots
description: Walk along extreme vertices of a convex feasible polytope and verify complementary slackness and strong KKT duality.

challenges.text: Rotate Objective Gradient (c₁, c₂) to trigger a vertex jump across an active facet.
Click inside the simplex to compare central-path interior trajectories vs boundary pivots.
Shrink Interior Barrier μ → 0 to drive the duality gap to zero.

name: Feigenbaum Period-Doubling & Logistic Bifurcation
description: Explore period-doubling cascades into chaos, cobweb orbits, and universal Feigenbaum scaling constants.

challenges.text: Sweep Growth Parameter r past 3.0, 3.449, and 3.5699 to witness period-2, 4, and chaos.
Click the phase space to seed two nearby orbits and measure Lyapunov divergence.
Locate the period-3 stability window near r ≈ 3.83.

name: Wavelet Time-Frequency Scalogram & Heisenberg Box
description: Trade off temporal vs spectral localization across dyadic Morlet/Haar wavelet scales and verify the Gabor uncertainty bound.

challenges.text: Adjust Dilation Scale a to stretch and compress the Heisenberg uncertainty box Δt·Δω ≥ 1/2.
Drag the time-frequency probe to localize a transient impulse.
Increase Dyadic Sub-bands J to resolve both high-frequency transients and low-frequency drift.

name: Topological Data Analysis & Vietoris-Rips Filtrations
description: Grow Vietoris-Rips balls of radius ε around a noisy point cloud and track Betti numbers β₀ (components) and β₁ (1-cycles).

challenges.text: Sweep Filtration Radius ε to observe the birth and death of the primary topological 1-cycle (β₁=1).
Drag a vertex on the simplicial complex to test topological stability under perturbation.
Filter out short-lived topological noise using Persistence Threshold τ.

name: Itô Stochastic Calculus & Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE
description: Simulate mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and geometric Brownian paths and verify the ½σ²f''(Xₜ)dt Itô correction term.

challenges.text: Increase Mean Reversion θ and confirm stationary variance shrinks as σ²/(2θ).
Click the phase canvas to launch an ensemble of sample paths from an extreme initial state.
Tune Volatility σ to observe the divergence between Itô and Stratonovich integrals.

name: p-Adic Valuation & Ultrametric Bruhat-Tits Tree
description: Explore non-Archimedean ultrametric balls in ℚ_p where every point inside a disk is its center and all triangles are isosceles.

challenges.text: Change Prime Base p to see p-ary branching across valuation levels.
Click a node to verify the strong triangle inequality |x+y|_p ≤ max(|x|_p, |y|_p).
Trace a Hensel-lifting root approximation down the p-adic tree.

name: Wasserstein Optimal Transport & Sinkhorn Entropic Plan
description: Compute entropically regularized Kantorovich transport plans via Sinkhorn-Knopp scaling and trace McCann displacement interpolations.

challenges.text: Decrease Entropic Regularization ε toward 0 to sharpen the coupling matrix into a deterministic Monge map.
Click the manifold to inspect the Wasserstein geodesic barycenter between source and target.
Vary Distribution Separation Δμ and verify quadratic scaling of W₂².

description: Compute the Fiedler vector v₂ of a weighted graph and partition nodes across the minimum-conductance spectral cut.

challenges.text: Lower Bottleneck Weight w_b and watch the Fiedler eigenvalue λ₂ approach zero.
Click a vertex to launch a heat-kernel diffusion wave e^{−tL}δᵢ.
Verify the Cheeger inequality connecting λ₂ to the sparse cut ratio h(G).

description: Compare straight-line, parabolic, and cycloid descent curves between two points under gravity to minimize travel time functional J[y].

challenges.text: Tune Path Cycloidicity α = 1.0 to achieve the stationary Euler-Lagrange minimum descent time.
Drag the bead along the curve to verify tautochrone isochronicity.
Add Kinetic Drag μ > 0 and find how friction shifts the optimal variational curve.

name: Schwarzschild Geodesics & Black Hole Gravitational Lensing
description: Integrate null and timelike geodesics around a Schwarzschild black hole to observe Einstein rings, the photon sphere at 1.5 r_s, and ISCO at 3 r_s.

challenges.text: Tune Impact Parameter b / r_s near √27/2 ≈ 2.60 to orbit the unstable photon sphere.
Click the orbital plane to change photon launch angle and observe relativistic deflection.
Increase Kerr Frame-Dragging a* to compare prograde vs retrograde ISCO radii.

name: Lagrangian Double Pendulum & Poincaré Section
description: Simulate the coupled Euler-Lagrange equations of a planar double pendulum transitioning from quasi-periodic KAM tori to Hamiltonian chaos.

challenges.text: Compare low-energy normal modes against high-energy chaotic flipping (E > 2.0).
Click the phase portrait to launch two nearly identical initial conditions.
Tune Mass Ratio m₂/m₁ to maximize momentum transfer between arms.

name: 2D Ising Model & Onsager Phase Transition
description: Run Metropolis-Hastings spin flips on a 2D ferromagnetic lattice across the critical Onsager temperature T_c ≈ 2.269 J/k_B.

challenges.text: Cool Temperature T/T_c below 1.0 to observe spontaneous magnetization symmetry breaking.
Click/drag on the spin lattice to nucleate a reversed Weiss magnetic domain.
Hold T/T_c = 1.0 to observe scale-invariant critical clusters and diverging susceptibility χ.

name: Maxwell Equations 2D FDTD & Evanescent Skin Depth
description: Propagate transverse electromagnetic waves across dielectric interfaces and conducting media to measure Fresnel reflection and skin depth δ.

challenges.text: Increase Permittivity ε_r to observe wavelength compression λ = λ₀/√ε_r.
Drag the field probe to measure standing-wave nodes and Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR).
Raise Conductivity Loss tan δ to observe exponential skin-depth attenuation.

name: Quantum Barrier Tunneling & WKB Transmission
description: Scatter a Gaussian Schrödinger wavepacket against a finite potential barrier and observe exponential WKB decay and Fabry-Pérot resonance.

challenges.text: Verify exponential sensitivity of transmission T when Barrier Width a doubles for E < V₀.
Click the state display to inject a coherent wavepacket superposition.
Tune Energy E / V₀ > 1.0 to locate a Ramsauer-Townsend transmission resonance where T = 1.

name: Carnot & Otto Thermodynamic P-V / T-S Engine
description: Trace isothermal and adiabatic strokes on coupled P-V and T-S diagrams and compare real irreversible efficiency against the Carnot bound.

challenges.text: Raise Reservoir Ratio T_H / T_C to increase maximum Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_C/T_H.
Drag the piston state marker along the isothermal expansion stroke.
Compare monatomic (γ=1.67) vs diatomic (γ=1.40) adiabatic slopes.

name: Navier-Stokes Vortex Shedding & Kármán Street
description: Simulate incompressible viscous flow past a cylindrical obstacle across Reynolds numbers Re and observe alternating Kármán vortex shedding.

challenges.text: Increase Reynolds Number Re past ~47 to trigger the Hopf bifurcation into periodic vortex shedding.
Click or drag in the wake to inject a vorticity perturbation.
Verify Strouhal number St ≈ 0.20 stability across moderate Reynolds numbers.

name: Rotating Reference Frame & Foucault Coriolis Precession
description: Track projectile and Foucault pendulum trajectories in a rotating planetary frame under Coriolis and centrifugal pseudo-forces.

challenges.text: Set Latitude φ = 90° (North Pole) vs φ = 0° (Equator) to verify precession rate Ω sin φ.
Click the horizontal plane to launch a rose-petal Coriolis trajectory.
Increase Planetary Rotation Ω to observe geostrophic cyclonic deflection.

name: Acoustic Doppler Shift & Supersonic Mach Shock Cone
description: Emit spherical wavefronts from a moving source and transition through the transonic barrier M = 1 into a conical Mach shock envelope.

challenges.text: Set Mach Number M = 1.0 to observe wavefront pileup at the sonic barrier.
Drag the observer microphone on the canvas to measure approaching vs receding Doppler shift.
Tune M = 2.0 and verify the Mach half-angle μ = arcsin(1/2) = 30°.

name: Driven RLC Resonator, Impedance Phasor & Bode Plot
description: Sweep AC drive frequency across LC resonance ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and inspect voltage/current phase lead-lag and quality factor Q.

challenges.text: Tune ω / ω₀ = 1.0 so inductive and capacitive reactances cancel (phase φ = 0°).
Drag the frequency probe to locate the −3 dB half-power bandwidth Δω = ω₀/Q.
Compare capacitive phase lead (ω < ω₀) vs inductive phase lag (ω > ω₀).

name: Bragg X-Ray Diffraction & Reciprocal Lattice Ewald Sphere
description: Scatter monochromatic X-rays off Miller crystal planes (hkl) and locate constructive Laue/Bragg peaks on the Ewald sphere.

challenges.text: Satisfy Bragg's law 2d sin θ = nλ for Cu-Kα (λ = 1.54 Å) to maximize peak intensity.
Drag the detector probe across 2θ to measure higher-order diffraction peaks (n=2, 3).
Decrease Lattice Spacing d and observe reciprocal-space expansion.

name: Two-Level Rabi Oscillations & Bloch Sphere Nutation
description: Drive a quantum two-level spin-1/2 system with an oscillating RF field and observe resonant Rabi flips and Ramsey detuning fringes.

challenges.text: Set Detuning Δ = 0 to achieve 100% population inversion P(|1⟩) = 1.0.
Click the Bloch sphere to apply an instantaneous π/2 Ramsey pulse.
Increase Detuning |Δ| and observe faster nutation Ω_eff with reduced inversion amplitude.

name: Bose-Einstein, Fermi-Dirac & Maxwell-Boltzmann Statistics
description: Compare quantum occupancy distributions across temperature T and chemical potential μ, from Fermi surfaces to Bose-Einstein condensation.

challenges.text: Cool k_B T / E_F → 0.02 to sharpen the degenerate Fermi step at ε = E_F.
Drag the energy probe across the thermal smearing window ~4 k_B T around μ.
Raise k_B T / E_F above 1.0 to see quantum statistics converge to classical Boltzmann tails.

name: Lorentz E×B Drift & Penning Ion Trap Trajectories
description: Confine charged particles using axial magnetic fields and quadrupole electrostatic potentials, decomposing cyclotron, magnetron, and axial modes.

challenges.text: Keep B₀ above the radial confinement limit ω_c² > 2ω_z² to prevent ion escape.
Click the trap cross-section to inject an ion and observe epitrochoid cyclotron+magnetron loops.
Vary q/m to separate isotopes by their modified cyclotron frequency ω₊.

name: Fresnel Equations, Brewster's Angle & Evanescent TIR
description: Plot s- and p-polarized reflectance R_s, R_p across incidence angle θᵢ, pinpointing Brewster's zero-glare angle and total internal reflection.

challenges.text: Drag the incidence angle cursor to Brewster's angle θ_B = arctan(n₂/n₁) where R_p = 0.
Set n₁ > n₂ (e.g. glass to air) to trigger Total Internal Reflection above θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁).
Compare s- vs p-polarized Fresnel reflection at grazing incidence.

name: 2D Biharmonic Chladni Plate Nodal Patterns
description: Excite flexural eigenmodes on a clamped/free square acoustic plate and watch sand grains migrate to zero-amplitude nodal lines.

challenges.text: Set distinct mode numbers (m ≠ n) to form symmetric/antisymmetric Chladni nodal figures.
Click on the plate to bow/pluck a local point and excite superposed eigenmodes.
Set m = n to collapse the degenerate pair into diagonal/circular nodes.

name: Superconducting Josephson Junction & Shapiro Steps
description: Simulate the resistively and capacitively shunted junction (RCSJ) washboard potential to observe DC/AC Josephson effects and quantized Shapiro voltage steps.

challenges.text: Keep Bias Current I / I_c < 1.0 to observe the zero-voltage DC supercurrent state.
Click the phase portrait to kick the superconducting phase φ over the washboard barrier.
Raise Microwave RF Drive A_rf with I > I_c to lock onto quantized Shapiro voltage steps.

name: Rayleigh-Bénard Thermal Convection & Boussinesq Rolls
description: Heat a fluid layer from below and observe the transition from conductive heat transfer to counter-rotating Bénard convection cells.

challenges.text: Raise Ra / Ra_c above 1.0 to trigger convective roll instability and raise Nusselt number Nu > 1.
Click the fluid layer to inject a buoyant thermal plume.
Vary Prandtl Number Pr to compare liquid-metal vs water/oil plume structures.

name: Anomalous Zeeman Effect & Atomic Multiplet Splitting
description: Apply an external magnetic field B to lift m_J degeneracy via Landé g-factor splitting and transition to the strong-field Paschen-Back regime.

challenges.text: Sweep Magnetic Field B from 0 to 5 T to watch spectral lines fan out linearly with m_J.
Drag the spectrometer probe to distinguish π (Δm=0) and σ± (Δm=±1) polarization components.
Increase B into the Paschen-Back regime where L and S decouple.

name: Quantum Vacuum Fluctuations & Casimir Plate Attraction
description: Quantize electromagnetic standing modes between uncharged conducting plates and compute the negative Casimir pressure from excluded vacuum modes.

challenges.text: Halve Plate Separation d and verify the 16× surge in Casimir attraction (∝ d⁻⁴).
Drag the cavity probe to inspect discrete intra-cavity modes vs continuum exterior modes.
Tune Plasma Cutoff ω_p to observe finite-conductivity skin-depth corrections.

name: Michaelis-Menten & Allosteric Hill Enzyme Kinetics
description: Analyze initial enzymatic reaction velocity v₀ vs substrate concentration [S] under competitive, uncompetitive, and cooperative Hill binding.

challenges.text: Increase K_m while holding V_max constant to simulate a competitive inhibitor.
Drag the substrate marker [S] to K_m and verify v₀ = 0.5 V_max.
Set Hill Cooperativity n_H ≥ 2.5 to turn the hyperbolic curve into a sigmoidal hemoglobin-like switch.

name: Nernst Galvanic Cell Potential & Concentration Polarization
description: Compute non-standard galvanic cell voltage E_cell as reaction quotient Q evolves toward equilibrium K_eq (where E = 0).

challenges.text: Change log₁₀(Q) by 1 unit at n=1 vs n=2 to verify the 59.2/n mV Nernst slope.
Drag the reaction coordinate along the discharge curve toward equilibrium E = 0 V.
