name: Stroop Task Lab
description: Play the classic Stroop task (Stroop, 1935): click the INK colour of each word as fast as you can. Your reaction times are measured per trial and split into congruent, neutral and incongruent trials to reveal the interference effect — automatic reading you cannot switch off.

challenges.text: Complete a colour-naming block with ≥ 80 % accuracy that shows a positive interference effect (incongruent slower than congruent).
Also run a word-reading block. Is interference much smaller when you just read the word? Why would that be?
Proportion-congruent effect: run colour-naming blocks at ≥ 75 % and ≤ 25 % congruent and compare interference.
Get a mean incongruent RT under 750 ms while staying ≥ 90 % accurate in a colour-naming block.

name: Signal Detection Theory Lab
description: Equal-variance Gaussian signal detection: drag the criterion across the noise and signal+noise distributions to trade hits against false alarms, watch the operating point slide along the ROC curve, and compute d′, c and β. Then switch to Play mode and judge noisy flashes yourself — your own d′ and bias are measured.

challenges.text: Drag the criterion to make the observer unbiased (c ≈ 0, β ≈ 1). Where does that sit relative to the two distributions?
Set P(signal) ≤ 0.2 and place the criterion within 0.1 of the β-optimal point. Why does a rare signal make the ideal observer conservative?
Set d′ = 0. What happens to the ROC curve, and why can no criterion help?
Play a 40-trial session and reach d′ ≥ 1.0 with your own eyes.

name: Rescorla–Wagner Conditioning Model
description: Pavlovian learning as error correction: ΔV = αβ(λ − ΣV) (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972). Pick a classic experimental design — acquisition/extinction, blocking, overshadowing, conditioned inhibition, overexpectation, or latent inhibition (a well-known failure of the pure model) — and watch the associative strengths of cues A and B evolve trial by trial.

options.label: Latent inhibition — NOT predicted by RW

challenges.text: In the blocking design, get V_B below 0.1·λ at the end while the control group's V_B exceeds 0.3·λ.
Create a conditioned inhibitor: make V_B fall below −0.3·λ.
Overshadowing: tune the saliences so that V_A ends more than 3× larger than V_B.
Overexpectation: show that reinforcing the AB compound makes ΣV drop by more than 0.1·λ.

name: Schedules of Reinforcement — Cumulative Recorder
description: A simulated lever-pressing rat on FR, VR, FI and VI schedules (Ferster & Skinner, 1957), drawn as a classic cumulative record: slope = response rate, ticks = reinforcers. See FR break-and-run with post-reinforcement pauses, FI scallops, steady VR/VI responding, and the extinction burst when reinforcement stops.

challenges.text: Run a Fixed-Interval schedule until ≥ 5 reinforcers have been earned and spot the 'scallop' — a pause, then accelerating responding.
Run VR and VI for ≥ 120 s each (sim time). Which produces the higher response rate, and why does a ratio schedule reward speed?
Switch on extinction after training and catch the extinction burst before responding dies out.
Raise the FR ratio until the mean post-reinforcement pause exceeds 8 s.

name: Serial Position & Free Recall
description: Study a list of words shown one at a time, then recall as many as you can in any order. Your recall by list position builds a serial-position curve — primacy and recency — compared against a two-store memory model. Add a distractor delay to replicate Glanzer & Cunitz (1966), or switch to simulate mode to explore the model.

challenges.text: Study and recall 3 lists, then compare your curve with the model's.
Show recency in your own data: after ≥ 3 immediate-recall lists, recall the last item better than the middle items.
In simulate mode add a 30-s distractor. Which end of the curve vanishes, and what does that say about short-term memory?
In simulate mode compare fast (≤ 750 ms) and slow (≥ 2500 ms) presentation. Which part of the curve does rate affect?

name: Forgetting Curve & Spaced Review
description: The forgetting curve, first measured by Ebbinghaus (1885) with his savings method, modelled here with the common exponential approximation R = e^(−t/S): retention decays with memory stability S. (Ebbinghaus's own fit was a different, logarithmic savings formula.) In this illustrative model every review boosts S — and more so when some forgetting has happened first (the spacing effect). Compare massed, cram, uniform and expanding schedules, or click the timeline to design your own.

challenges.text: With the same number (≥ 2) of reviews, show that expanding spaced reviews beat massed day-0 reviews by ≥ 30 points on test day.

Click the timeline to build a custom schedule with at most 4 reviews that gives ≥ 80 % retention on test day AND still ≥ 45 % 30 days after the test (default S₀ and gain; the expanding preset only manages ≈ 39 %).
Try cramming the night before. Test-day retention looks fine — but what is left 30 days after the test?
Set the initial stability so that the one-shot half-life (S₀·ln 2) is ≈ 1 day.

name: Psychophysics: Weber's Law & JND Staircase
description: Measure your own just-noticeable difference: which line (or patch) is bigger? A 1-up/2-down adaptive staircase homes in on the difference you detect 70.7 % of the time, giving your Weber fraction k = ΔI/I. Then compare Fechner's logarithmic law with Stevens' power law across sensory continua.

params.label: Standard magnitude I (px or grey level)

challenges.text: Run a staircase to completion and read off your Weber fraction.
Test Weber's law: measure k at two standards at least 2× apart (same stimulus type) and get Weber fractions within a factor of 1.5.
Set the exponent to electric shock (3.5): doubling the current multiplies felt intensity by about 11. Why might that be adaptive?
Find the Stevens exponent whose power curve best mimics Fechner's log law over I = 1…100.

name: Visual Search: Feature vs Conjunction
description: Is there a red vertical bar? A simplified version of Treisman & Gelade's (1980) search paradigm (they used coloured letters and shapes). In feature search the target differs by colour alone and 'pops out'; in conjunction search it shares colour with some distractors and orientation with others. Your RT × set-size slopes (ms/item) reveal efficient (parallel-like) vs inefficient (serial-like) search.

options.label: Conjunction (red vertical among green vertical + red horizontal)

challenges.text: Complete one feature block and one conjunction block.
Show pop-out: get a feature-search target-present slope below 10 ms/item (≥ 12 correct present trials).
Show serial search: conjunction target-present slope above 10 ms/item, with the target-absent slope steeper still.

name: Mental Rotation (Shepard & Metzler)
description: Are the two shapes the same object rotated, or mirror images? Answer as fast as you can. Shepard & Metzler (1971), using 3-D block figures, found reaction time grows linearly with the angle between them — as if you rotate a mental image at a constant speed. Here you judge flat 2-D shapes rotated in the picture plane (as in Cooper & Shepard, 1973); your RT = a + b·angle fit gives your own rotation rate in degrees per second.

challenges.text: Complete a block with ≥ 80 % accuracy.
Show the linear angle effect: positive slope with r ≥ 0.7 across your angle means (≥ 4 angles).
Compare: are your correct 'mirror' responses slower than 'same' responses? (≥ 5 of each)

name: Prospect Theory & Framing
description: Kahneman & Tversky's prospect theory (1979; cumulative version, Tversky & Kahneman, 1992): outcomes are valued as gains or losses from a reference point with an S-shaped value function (concave for gains, convex and steeper for losses), and probabilities are distorted by a weighting function. Defaults are the 1992 median estimates (α = β = 0.88, λ = 2.25, γ = 0.61, δ = 0.69). Make the choices yourself — including the famous Asian-disease framing problem (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981) — and compare with the model's predictions and expected value.

challenges.text: Answer both Asian-disease frames yourself. The options are numerically identical — did your choice flip with the wording?
Turn the model into an expected-value maximiser (α = β = λ = γ = δ = 1). What happens to the framing effect?
In the mixed gamble, find the loss aversion λ at which the model is just indifferent between accepting and declining.
Fourfold pattern: show the model is risk-seeking for the long-shot lottery but risk-averse (buys insurance) for the small-probability loss.

name: Drift-Diffusion Decision Lab
description: Ratcliff's (1978) drift-diffusion model of two-choice decisions (all data simulated). Evidence follows a Wiener process dX = v·dt + s·dW (Euler–Maruyama, dt = 1 ms; s = 0.1 is Ratcliff's scaling convention) from start point z·a (measured from the lower boundary) until it hits the upper boundary (defined as the 'correct' response) or the lower ('error') one; RT = decision time + non-decision time Ter. Closed forms: P(upper) = (1 − e^(−2v·za/s²)) / (1 − e^(−2v·a/s²)) and E[DT] = (a·P(upper) − za)/v. A negative v models a stimulus that favours the lower response. Trials unfinished after 10 s are counted as timeouts.

params.label: Start point z (fraction of a; 0.5 = unbiased)

challenges.text: Speed–accuracy tradeoff: changing ONLY the boundary separation a (same v, z, s, Ter), collect ≥200 trials at a cautious boundary and ≥200 at a hasty one so accuracy differs by ≥8 points and mean RT by ≥80 ms (sessions are saved when you change a parameter).
With an unbiased start (z ≈ 0.5), show that correct and error RTs have the same mean (within 25 ms, ≥100 errors). Lower the drift to get errors faster.
Produce 'fast errors' (error RT ≥40 ms faster than correct RT, ≥30 errors, positive drift) by moving only the start point. Which way must z move?
Set the drift to 0: show that P(upper response) then equals the start point z (≥300 trials, within 6 points).

name: Asch Conformity: Line Judgement & Social Impact
description: Take part in a simulated Asch (1951, 1956) line-judgement study: computer 'confederates' answer before you and, on 12 of 18 trials, they are unanimously wrong. Then switch to 'Population model' to fit Latané's (1981) social impact law I = s·N^t (t < 1; t ≈ 0.5 is a commonly cited estimate) against approximate Asch conformity-vs-majority-size data. Model curves and the cohort are simulated, not data.

challenges.text: Complete all 18 trials of the line-judgement session (12 are critical).
Population model: tune t, s, μ and independents until the model fits the (approximate) Asch data with RMSE ≤ 5 percentage points.
Population model with N ≥ 3: switch on a single dissenter and make modelled conformity collapse to ≤ 12% from ≥ 25% (Asch 1955: a truthful partner cut errors to about a quarter, ≈ 5.5%).
Find settings where going from 4 to 15 confederates adds less than 5 points of conformity (diminishing marginal impact).

name: Big Five Psychometrics Lab
description: Simulated respondents answer a hypothetical 20-item Big Five (OCEAN) inventory (1–5 scale) generated from true factor loadings plus noise. Inspect the item correlation heatmap, the scree plot (Jacobi eigenvalues of the correlation matrix, with Kaiser's eigenvalue > 1 rule and Horn's parallel analysis) and Cronbach's α = k/(k−1)·(1 − Σσ²ᵢ/σ²_total) per scale (reverse-keyed items rescored as 6 − x). Then take the published 10-item TIPI (Gosling, Rentfrow & Swann 2003; 7-point scale, items 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 reverse-scored as 8 − x) and see your radar profile.

challenges.text: Get a clean solution: exactly 5 eigenvalues > 1 (Kaiser) and every scale α ≥ 0.70.
Turn off reverse-scoring with ≥2 reverse-keyed items per scale and watch α collapse below 0.40 for some scale.
Raise the item noise (above the default 0.8) until parallel analysis retains fewer than 5 factors.
Answer all 10 TIPI items and view your radar profile against the norms.

name: Replication Crisis Lab: Power, p-Hacking & Publication Bias
description: Simulate thousands of two-group experiments (pooled-variance Student t-tests, df = n₁ + n₂ − 2, exact p-values from the regularized incomplete beta function). See how true effect size d, sample size and α determine power (e.g. d = 0.5 needs ≈ 64 per group for 80% power at α = .05); switch on p-hacking practices to watch the false-positive rate inflate (Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn 2011 found up to ≈ 61% when four practices were combined); add publication bias and inspect the funnel plot and the winner's curse. All studies are simulated.

params.label: p-hack: optional stopping (add 10/group, up to 3 extra looks)

challenges.text: With d = 0 and no p-hacking, run ≥1000 studies and confirm the false-positive rate ≈ α (within 1.5 points of 5%).
With d = 0, combine ≥2 p-hacking practices to push the false-positive rate to ≥12% (Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn 2011).
Choose n so that a true d = 0.5 is detected with ≥80% observed power (≥500 studies, α = .05, no hacking). Tip: switch off 'Studies vary in size' to test one n exactly.
Winner's curse: with publication bias, a small true effect (0 < d ≤ 0.3) and n ≤ 30, get a mean published d at least twice the true d.

name: Infant Habituation & Dishabituation
description: A simulated infant-controlled habituation procedure (Horowitz et al. 1972; Horowitz 1974). Looking time to a repeated stimulus declines as the infant builds an internal representation (Sokolov's 1963 comparator model: the orienting response is driven by mismatch between input and the stored model). Once the mean of 3 consecutive trials falls below criterion (commonly 50% of the first 3 trials), test trials show recovery to a novel stimulus — or, in the violation-of-expectation framing of Baillargeon, Spelke & Wasserman (1985, 5-month-olds, rotating-screen 'drawbridge'), longer looking at an 'impossible' event. That interpretation is debated: Bogartz et al. (1997) and Rivera, Wakeley & Langer (1999) argued that perceptual/familiarity preferences can explain the effect (infants looked longer at the 180° rotation even with no box). Looking times here are model output, not data.

options.label: Violation of expectation (drawbridge, Baillargeon et al. 1985)

challenges.text: Make an infant reach the habituation criterion within 6 trials (the earliest possible: 3 baseline + 3 criterion trials).
Make the novel stimulus so similar (≥0.9) that recovery is under 1 s — a null result that does NOT prove infants can't tell them apart.
Produce a novelty preference ≥ 70% (novel / (novel + familiar) looking).

Violation of expectation (model): get the 'impossible' event looked at ≥2 s longer than the 'possible' one, even though it is perceptually MORE similar to the habituation event. Then ask: what non-'knowledge' explanation could critics offer?

name: Exposure Therapy: Habituation, Extinction & Avoidance
description: An illustrative computational sketch (not a validated clinical model) of exposure in the spirit of inhibitory-learning theory (Craske et al. 2008, 2014). Fear (SUDS 0–100) = threat association E × (1 − inhibitory learning I) × exposure intensity. While the person stays in the situation and the feared outcome does not occur, I grows with the expectancy violation (expected threat ∝ intensity·E·(1−I), a Rescorla–Wagner-style prediction error). Within-session fear decline (the habituation time constant) changes how sessions feel but is NOT required for long-term success — in line with Craske et al.'s finding that within-session habituation does not predict outcome. Escaping early is negatively reinforced and leaves the threat belief unchallenged; safety behaviours let the person credit the behaviour rather than the situation, reducing learning. Follow-up probes spontaneous recovery (time) and renewal (a context other than the therapy context; reinstatement is not modelled).

challenges.text: Run avoidance for ≥6 sessions: escaping brings quick relief, yet fear at follow-up is as high as ever.
With graded exposure (no safety behaviours), get follow-up peak SUDS below 40 (hint: more sessions or a faster inhibitory-learning rate η).
Show that safety behaviours undermine exposure: follow-up SUDS ≥15 points higher with them than without.
Renewal: after successful exposure, test in a new context and see fear return by ≥20 SUDS relative to the final session.

name: Hick–Hyman Choice Reaction Time Game
description: Play a choice reaction-time task: after a random 0.6–1.8 s foreperiod one of N equiprobable targets lights up — hit it as fast as you can (keys 1–8 are best; mouse clicks add movement time). RT is timed with performance.now() from the animation frame that draws the target (display lag of ~1 frame is not corrected); responses during the foreperiod are false starts, RTs < 100 ms are excluded as anticipations and > 3 s as lapses. Mean RTs are fitted to the Hick–Hyman law in Hick's (1952) form RT = a + b·log2(N + 1), where the +1 reflects uncertainty about whether/when a stimulus occurs (Hyman 1953 used log2 N, the stimulus information). Fitts mode uses MacKenzie's (1992) Shannon formulation MT = a + b·log2(D/W + 1) (Fitts' 1954 original: log2(2D/W)).

challenges.text: Collect ≥5 valid trials at each of 3 different set sizes N.
With ≥4 set sizes, get a Hick–Hyman fit with positive slope and R² ≥ 0.8 (on the mean RTs).
Simple reaction time: mean RT under 350 ms at N = 1 (≥5 trials).
Fitts mode: ≥12 hits across ≥3 indices of difficulty with R² ≥ 0.7 (fit to the mean MT per ID, as is conventional).

name: Visual Illusions: Method of Adjustment
description: Psychophysics by the method of adjustment: drag the comparison until it looks equal to the standard, then submit (trials alternate ascending/descending starts). Your point of subjective equality (PSE) gives the illusion magnitude in %. Müller-Lyer: outward fins (tails) lengthen and arrowheads shorten the shaft; typical magnitudes are roughly 10–30% depending on fin length and angle, larger with more acute fins. Ponzo: of two equal lines between converging rails, the one nearer the apex looks longer. Ebbinghaus: a centre circle surrounded by large circles looks smaller, by small circles larger.

params.label: Context strength (fin length / rail tilt / inducer size)

challenges.text: Measure the Müller-Lyer PSE at ≥3 fin angles, including one below 60° and one above 120°.
Show the illusion reverses sign: positive mean error for outward fins (<90°) and negative for arrowheads (>90°).
At 90° (perpendicular fins) get a mean illusion within ±5% (≥2 matches).
Record at least one match in both the Ponzo and the Ebbinghaus illusion.

name: N-Back Working-Memory Task
description: Play the n-back task: respond 'Match' whenever the current item (a letter or a grid position) is the same as the one n steps back. 30% of scored trials are targets. Performance is scored with signal-detection theory: d′ = z(H) − z(FA) using the log-linear correction (Hautus 1995: add 0.5 to hits and false alarms and 1 to the numbers of signal and noise trials). Note that percent correct is inflated by the 70% non-targets (never responding scores ≈ 70%), which is why d′ is preferred. Adaptive mode raises n when accuracy ≥ 80% and d′ ≥ 1.

challenges.text: Complete a full block.
Reach d′ ≥ 2 in a block.
Score ≥80% accuracy with d′ ≥ 1 at n ≥ 2 (d′ stops you winning by never responding).
Complete a 3-back block with d′ ≥ 1.

name: Two-Process Model of Sleep Regulation
description: Borbély's (1982) two-process model as formalised by Daan, Beersma & Borbély (1984): homeostatic sleep pressure S rises exponentially toward an upper asymptote during wake (τ ≈ 18.2 h) and decays during sleep (τ ≈ 4.2 h), while circadian Process C (here a pure 24 h sinusoid; the original used a skewed waveform) modulates the upper (sleep-onset) and lower (waking) thresholds (illustrative values 0.60 and 0.17 ± 0.12). Explore sleep deprivation, chronotype and caffeine. Caffeine is an adenosine A1/A2A receptor antagonist with a half-life of ≈ 5 h in adults (≈ 3–7 h typical); here it is modelled — as a deliberate simplification — by subtracting a saturating term from 'felt' S while true S keeps rising. The alertness index is a relative, illustrative quantity.

params.label: Sleep deprivation on night 1 (extra hours awake)
Caffeine per day (mg; t½ = 5 h model)

challenges.text: Pull an all-nighter (≥20 h extra) and see S rise above the sleep threshold — sleep propensity is then very high and microsleeps become more likely.

After ≥12 h of deprivation, use ≥200 mg caffeine to raise the (model) alertness index by ≥10 points at some waking moment — then notice that, in this simplified masking model, S itself keeps rising unchanged.
Make the alarm cut sleep short by ≥1.5 h compared with waking naturally (hint: an owl chronotype with an early alarm).
With the alarm off, show that recovery sleep after ≥16 h deprivation lasts ≥1 h longer than your planned sleep.
